html:
The siege of Pavia lasted from September 773 to June 774 at Pavia, the Lombard capital, in northern Italy. Charlemagne, king of the Franks, took the city and the Lombard kingdom with it.

The Lombards had ruled most of Italy for two centuries and kept pressing on the lands of the pope. Their king Desiderius seized papal towns and threatened Rome. He also sheltered the widow and young sons of Charlemagne's brother, who had a claim to the Frankish throne. Pope Adrian I asked Charlemagne for help. The Franks crossed the Alps in two columns, got around the Lombard defences in the mountain passes, and shut Desiderius up in Pavia. They had no siege engines, so they waited. Charlemagne spent Easter in Rome while the blockade went on. Hunger and disease forced the city to give up.

Desiderius was sent to a monastery, and Charlemagne took the title king of the Lombards himself. The Lombard kingdom ended, though Lombard dukes held on in the south. Charlemagne confirmed the pope's lands, the start of the Papal States, and tied the papacy to the Franks. That bond led to his crowning as emperor in 800.
